question: What is the primary focus of non-pain symptom management in palliative care?

options.A: Speeding up the natural dying process safely
options.B: Curing the underlying terminal disease process
options.C: Eliminating the need for any medications
options.D: Maximizing patient comfort and quality of life

explanation: Palliative care focuses on comfort and quality of life when a cure is no longer possible. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T15#GNS321_U4_T15_h1)

question: Why are non-pain symptoms considered just as important to manage as pain in palliative patients?

options.A: They are always much easier to treat than physical pain
options.B: They never respond to standard nursing interventions
options.C: They can cause severe physical and emotional distress
options.D: They indicate that the patient has exactly one week to live

explanation: Symptoms like breathlessness or fatigue significantly drain a patient's reserves and peace of mind. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T15#GNS321_U4_T15_h1)

question: Why is a single initial assessment insufficient for palliative care patients?

options.A: Palliative conditions and symptoms change rapidly over time
options.B: Patients usually forget their medical history on day one
options.C: Doctors prefer to change diagnoses daily without reason
options.D: Hospitals require a new paperwork form every single hour

explanation: Because disease trajectories fluctuate, ongoing re-assessment is necessary to catch new or worsening symptoms. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T15#GNS321_U4_T15_h2)

question: What does a holistic evaluation of a palliative patient include?

options.A: Surgical history and previous childhood illnesses only
options.B: Only laboratory test results and vital sign trends
options.C: Physical, psychological, social, and spiritual well-being
options.D: Financial statements and insurance coverage limits

explanation: Holistic care addresses every aspect of a person's life, recognizing that emotional and spiritual pain affects physical comfort. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T15#GNS321_U4_T15_h2)

question: What is the best way to prevent opioid-induced constipation in palliative patients?

options.A: Encourage the patient to eat three large meals every day
options.B: Start prophylactic laxatives at the same time as the opioid
options.C: Wait until the patient complains of severe abdominal pain
options.D: Stop the opioid medication immediately at the first dose

explanation: Opioids slow down the bowel permanently, so preventative laxatives must be prescribed right away rather than reacting after constipation occurs. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T15#GNS321_U4_T15_h3)

question: A patient on strong pain medication reports feeling constantly queasy and unable to keep food down. What is the nurse's best initial action?

options.A: Administer a strong laxative immediately to clear the bowels
options.B: Identify the specific trigger to select the correct antiemetic
options.C: Force the patient to finish a standard hospital meal tray
options.D: Advise the patient to completely stop drinking all water

explanation: Different antiemetics work on different pathways in the body, so finding the cause ensures the right medication is given. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T15#GNS321_U4_T15_h3)

question: Why might a palliative patient feel severely short of breath even when their oxygen saturation is normal?

options.A: Pulse oximeters always give false readings in terminally ill patients
options.B: The patient is only pretending to panic to gain attention
options.C: Dyspnea is a subjective feeling influenced by many physical and emotional factors
options.D: Normal oxygen levels mean the lungs are working at full capacity

explanation: Breathlessness is a personal sensation that does not always match objective lab or monitor readings. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T15#GNS321_U4_T15_h4)

question: Which simple non-pharmacological nursing intervention often helps relieve sudden breathlessness?

options.A: Placing the patient flat on their back without a pillow
options.B: Closing all windows and doors to trap warm indoor air
options.C: Asking the patient to hold their breath for one minute
options.D: Directing a cool fan or breeze across the patient's face

explanation: Stimulating the trigeminal nerve with cool airflow helps trick the brain into feeling like breathing is easier. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T15#GNS321_U4_T15_h4)

question: How does palliative fatigue differ from normal everyday tiredness?

options.A: It only occurs during the first few hours of the morning
options.B: It can always be cured by eating a high-protein meal
options.C: It is caused strictly by a lack of physical exercise
options.D: It does not improve with rest or a good night's sleep

explanation: Palliative fatigue is a deep, systemic exhaustion rooted in the underlying disease process rather than simple lack of sleep. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T15#GNS321_U4_T15_h5)

question: A distressed family member is upset because their dying relative refuses to eat meals. What is the most appropriate nursing response?

options.A: Scold the patient for not trying hard enough to maintain their body weight
options.B: Tell the family to force feed the patient large portions using a syringe
options.C: Explain that declining appetite is a natural part of the illness and focus on mouth care
options.D: Insist that the doctor order total parenteral nutrition immediately

explanation: Reassuring the family and shifting attention away from forced feeding reduces anxiety for everyone involved. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T15#GNS321_U4_T15_h5)

question: What is a crucial first step when a palliative patient suddenly develops acute delirium?

options.A: Double the dose of all routine daily medications
options.B: Instantly tie the patient's hands to the bed rails for safety
options.C: Turn off all lights and leave the patient completely alone
options.D: Search for and treat reversible underlying triggers like infection or pain

explanation: Delirium is often a symptom of an underlying physical issue like a UTI, constipation, or hypoxia that needs correction. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T15#GNS321_U4_T15_h6)

question: Which environmental strategy helps manage a confused and restless patient experiencing delirium?

options.A: Playing loud, fast-paced music to keep their attention focused
options.B: Keeping the room quiet and well-lit with familiar personal items nearby
options.C: Restricting all family members from visiting to prevent stimulation
options.D: Constantly moving the patient to a brand new room every shift

explanation: A calm, recognizable environment reduces fear and disorientation in patients with altered mental status. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T15#GNS321_U4_T15_h6)

question: What is a common non-pharmacological comfort measure for a patient suffering from severe itching (pruritus)?

options.A: Applying hot heating pads directly over the itchy rash
options.B: Encouraging the patient to scratch freely with long nails
options.C: Scrubbing the dry skin vigorously with a rough washcloth
options.D: Applying cool compresses to the affected itchy areas

explanation: Cool temperatures help soothe nerve endings that transmit the sensation of itch without breaking the skin. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T15#GNS321_U4_T15_h7)

question: Why are palliative patients at such high risk for developing pressure injuries?

options.A: Poor mobility, reduced tissue perfusion, and loss of subcutaneous fat
options.B: They sweat excessively due to high room temperatures
options.C: They consume too many high-fat foods in their daily diet
options.D: Skin cells multiply at a dangerously fast rate near the end of life

explanation: Decreased blood flow, immobility, and wasting tissues make the skin fragile and vulnerable to breakdown. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T15#GNS321_U4_T15_h7)

question: Why is a multidisciplinary team essential in palliative symptom management?

options.A: Doctors are not allowed to speak directly with family members
options.B: Complex physical and emotional symptoms require varied professional expertise
options.C: Hospital regulations state that five nurses must see every patient
options.D: It prevents nurses from having to perform any physical assessments

explanation: No single discipline can address every physical, psychological, and spiritual need of a dying patient. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T15#GNS321_U4_T15_h8)

question: What is the primary role of the nurse within the multidisciplinary palliative care team?

options.A: Making all final medical diagnoses and prescribing drugs alone
options.B: Replacing the family members during visiting hours
options.C: Acting as a central hub of communication and coordinating care
options.D: Handling the financial billing and insurance claims for the hospital

explanation: Nurses spend the most time at the bedside, making them uniquely positioned to coordinate input from all team members. [learn more](GNS321_U4_T15#GNS321_U4_T15_h8)
